The maximum total length attained by the capitán (Eremophilus mutisii) has been recorded as 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger members of the Trichomycteridae. This ultimate length represents the upper end of the size range observed in wild populations inhabiting the high-altitude streams of the Colombian Andes. Field surveys indicate that individuals typically require several years to approach this asymptotic size, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of sexual maturation. The body proportions of a fully grown adult, including a robust head and a laterally compressed caudal peduncle, reflect its benthic feeding habits in fast-flowing, well-oxygenated waters. A gravid female of this size can carry a substantial ovarian mass, underscoring the species' reproductive investment relative to its body plan. Comparisons with congeneric species suggest that this maximum length is correlated with the thermal regime of its native páramo environment, where cool waters constrain metabolic rates and thus prolong the growth phase.

Sexual maturation in Eremophilus mutisii is achieved at a relatively modest body size, with the total length at puberty reported as 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters]. Individuals reaching this threshold exhibit the first signs of gonadal recrudescence, including the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 8.6 grams [Wwp = 8.6 grams], a value derived from a length-weight relationship typical of this species. Achieving this size generally coincides with the second or third year of life, depending on local food availability and water temperature. The relatively small size at maturity suggests that E. mutisii prioritizes early reproductive output over extended somatic growth, a life-history tactic that may be adaptive in variable high-elevation habitats where adult mortality can be unpredictable. Once mature, individuals continue to grow, though at a reduced rate, eventually reaching the much larger adult dimensions that characterize the oldest members of the population.

Reproduction in the capitán is characterized by a high fecundity strategy, with females producing approximately 55.7 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 55.7 eggs per spawning event] and spawning approximately 365 times each year [F_R_i = approximately 365 times each year] under the thermal conditions found in its native habitat, where water temperatures average 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This annual reproductive timetable aligns with the seasonal flooding cycles of Andean streams, which provide ample nursery habitat for the developing larvae. The daily rate of offspring production derived from these figures is not directly recorded but is implicit in the batch fecundity and spawning frequency. Each fertilized ovum is quite small, reflecting an initial investment per offspring that is modest yet sufficient for lecithotrophic development. The combination of moderate clutch size and an extended breeding interval suggests that E. mutisii balances the energetic demands of gamete production with the need to maintain body condition in an oligotrophic environment.

The early developmental stages of Eremophilus mutisii are critically dependent on ambient temperature, with embryogenesis proceeding rapidly at warmer conditions. At 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a temperature commonly recorded in the cooler headwaters of its range, the time from fertilization to larval eclosion lasts approximately 6.7 days [ab = approximately 6.7 days]. This age at birth is relatively short for a trichomycterid fish, likely an adaptation to reduce the window of vulnerability during the egg stage. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are minute, with an average wet weight at birth of only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = only 0.00052 grams], a value that corresponds to the small diameter of the adhesive, demersal eggs. These lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching before the mouth opens and the gut differentiates, marking the onset of exogenous feeding. The rapid progression from egg to free-swimming larva minimizes the risk of predation on the vulnerable embryonic stages within the gravel nests.

Under the warmer thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum lifespan of Eremophilus mutisii has been documented at 8 years [am = 8 years], a longevity that is substantial for a fish of its relatively small ultimate wet weight of 172.5 grams [Wwi = 172.5 grams]. The oldest individuals captured in long-term population surveys exhibit eroded fin margins and reduced growth increments, confirming the onset of senescence. This maximum age is comparable to that of other Andean siluriforms that inhabit stable, low-predation environments. The species' extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive events across several years, reinforcing an iteroparous life-history strategy. Interestingly, the 172.5 gram [Wwi = 172.5 gram] maximum mass represents a dramatic increase over the pubertal weight, illustrating a substantial post-maturation growth phase that continues well after the onset of gonadal activity.
